question: Read Figure B.4.1.1: how many immediate productivity-component branches leave the Human Capital Index root, and which single leaf is attached to the Survival component?
answer:
Three immediate productivity-component branches leave the Human Capital Index root. [p135-figure-B.4.1.1]

The single leaf attached to the Survival component is Survival to age 5. [p135-figure-B.4.1.1]

Note: Ratio of average outcomes between children in the richest quintile (Q1) and the poorest quintile (Q5), according to the 2013 Human Capital Index (HCI)
disaggregated by socioeconomic status (SES).
Source: World Bank 2019b.




      BOX                  4.1.          World Bank’s human capital index


    The World Bank created the Human Capital Index (HCI) to assess the conditions that will shape the productivity
    of the next generation (Kraay, 2018). The HCI is part of a broader World Bank Group initiative that emphasizes and
    prioritizes investment in people. By anchoring the index in economic theory, it raises awareness of the opportunity cost of
    inaction and bolsters demand for effective interventions. To accelerate evidence-based investments in people for greater equity
    and growth, the HCI benchmarks the accumulation of human capital across the world. The index provides an indicator for
    how the current level of health and education will impact productivity in the next generation of workers.

    The HCI encompasses key health measures, including survival, education, and health. These three broad categories
    are measured through the under-5 mortality rate, the under-5 stunting rate, and the survival rate for adults aged 15–60. It also
    estimates the quantity and quality of education by measuring learning-adjusted years of schooling—the expected number of
    years of schooling received by age 18, adjusted to reflect educational quality as proxied by standardized test scores. The HCI
    benchmarks different aspects of human capital including education (expected years of schooling and harmonized test scores)
    and health (child survival, child stunting, and adult survival rates). These composite indicators are combined to estimate the
    expected productivity of a child born today as a future worker relative to a benchmark of complete education and full health.

original pixels and record page coordinates. Inspect the full page if a crop
misses a needed heading, note or neighboring object.
Read table
headers, row, column, unit and year carefully. Read diagram arrows/branches and
chart legends/axes from images; layout text alone can lose relationships.
Match each legend label to its color, then read the marks at the EXACT requested
category or date. A comparison can reverse between categories. For close marks,
compare their heights against the same baseline, not the overall trend.
For table questions, use the precision displayed in the cells rather than a
rounded number from nearby prose. Include price year and currency/denominator
from table headers when applicable. If asked for a color, name its legend color.
If a visual relationship or value is unclear, inspect its page rather than guess.
For multi-page questions retrieve and cite EACH necessary page. Compute only from
visible values, distinguish percent from percentage points. Answer only the asked
facts. For probabilities on a 0-to-1 scale, a difference in percentage points is
100 times the probability difference. For values already expressed as percent,
subtract directly. An index-point difference remains index points, not percent.
Preserve qualifications, avoid unsupported extra claims. Never treat a
projection as an observed survey result. If the exact requested data are absent,
abstain explicitly without speculation, even when a related number is present.
You may call search/inspect_pages together when their remaining limits allow it.
Each inspect_pages call accepts up to two pages; prefer a single call for two
pages. Call finish by itself, with status answered or
abstain. For answered, provide claims with text and
evidence_ids. Each evidence ID MUST identify a source image actually shown in the
CURRENT_CONTEXT, not just text returned by search. Use inspect_pages if needed.
Do not provide supports, modes or text quotes in this image-citation protocol.
Read the claim from the original image; the renderer only checks image presence,
not whether its meaning is correct. For a numerical change, give approximate
values and units at the requested endpoints as well as direction. Preserve the
price year, denominator, legend color and every requested qualification.
Do not put citation markers in claim text. For abstain, claims must be empty and
abstention_reason must explain the missing evidence. Before declaring a named
source absent, search its exact Table/Figure label and inspect its page if found.

are current. A source present as text but without its image is not missing from
the report: inspect it before answering. Always call finish; a plain assistant
message is not a submitted answer. Use the question's language.

      BOX                  4.1.          World Bank’s human capital index


    The World Bank created the Human Capital Index (HCI) to assess the conditions that will shape the productivity
    of the next generation (Kraay, 2018). The HCI is part of a broader World Bank Group initiative that emphasizes and
    prioritizes investment in people. By anchoring the index in economic theory, it raises awareness of the opportunity cost of
    inaction and bolsters demand for effective interventions. To accelerate evidence-based investments in people for greater equity
    and growth, the HCI benchmarks the accumulation of human capital across the world. The index provides an indicator for
    how the current level of health and education will impact productivity in the next generation of workers.

    The HCI encompasses key health measures, including survival, education, and health. These three broad categories
    are measured through the under-5 mortality rate, the under-5 stunting rate, and the survival rate for adults aged 15–60. It also
    estimates the quantity and quality of education by measuring learning-adjusted years of schooling—the expected number of
    years of schooling received by age 18, adjusted to reflect educational quality as proxied by standardized test scores. The HCI
    benchmarks different aspects of human capital including education (expected years of schooling and harmonized test scores)
    and health (child survival, child stunting, and adult survival rates). These composite indicators are combined to estimate the
    expected productivity of a child born today as a future worker relative to a benchmark of complete education and full health.
